site.name: Positive
site.intro: Five small retellings from India’s living story traditions. Read one, then return to your day a little lighter.

stories.title: The Princess of Three Breasts
stories.source: Panchatantra — Arthur W. Ryder translation (1925), Internet Archive
body: In a far-off kingdom, the king's daughter was born with three breasts, and the court astrologers foretold that her unusual form would change the moment she met her destined husband. The king raised her with care, shielding her until the proper suitor should appear.

When a poor but willing young man agreed to marry her, the wedding was held with quiet hope. On the night they were united, the princess's third breast vanished, and the astrologers' prophecy was fulfilled at last.

The husband, content with such grace, sought nothing more, and his bride became a cherished queen. Together they brought prosperity to the realm, turning what had seemed a strange misfortune into a joyful marriage and a stable kingdom.

stories.title: The Elephant's Friend Returns Home
stories.source: More Jataka Tales — Ellen C. Babbitt (1922), Project Gutenberg
body: Beside the royal elephant's stable, a small dog became a daily companion, sharing meals and play, their contentment plain to every groom. When a stranger bought the dog and led him away, the great elephant refused his food and his bath, standing listless in his stall while his friend grew further with every passing hour.

The king, seeing his prized animal pining, sent a wise man to seek the cause. By quietly watching the elephant's longing gaze and tracing the trail to the buyer, the wise man brought word back to the palace. The king, recognizing such true affection, ordered the little dog returned at once to his grieving friend.

Reunited in the warm stable, the dog pressed close and the elephant trumpeted softly, both whole again as they shared their meal. Their bond, honored by the king himself, became a small but lasting promise: that kindness between even the most unlikely friends is seen, remembered, and protected.

stories.title: Two Souls Released by One Cry
body: At the lotus-filled lake where his herd drank, Gajendra the elephant king suddenly felt a crocodile lock onto his leg. His companions trumpeted and pulled, but the grip held firm, and one long, exhausting struggle wore him down. At last he remembered a prayer from a former life and, raising a lotus in his trunk, called sincerely to the Supreme Lord.

The heavens answered. Vishnu arrived on his great eagle Garuda, swift and radiant, and severed the crocodile's ancient jaws. Two beings were freed that day: Gajendra, who received liberation and the Lord's eternal companionship, and the crocodile himself, an old curse broken as he rose back into his true celestial form.

Even in overwhelming danger, a single heartfelt cry was heard. The story leaves a warm assurance that no struggle is too heavy and no moment too late for grace to descend, lifting both the one who calls and the one who waits to be released.

stories.title: A Garland in the Hall of Drupada
stories.source: Mahabharata — Adi Parva, Kisari Mohan Ganguli translation
body: In disguise, the five Pandava brothers and their mother entered the great hall where King Drupada had set an impossible test. A heavy bow waited beside a target, and proud kings from distant kingdoms had already failed to lift or string it, their laughter fading into uneasy silence.

Arjuna stepped forward in his simple brahmin's guise and strung the great bow with steady hands, striking the target by its reflection as the crowd watched in disbelief. Princess Draupadi rose and placed the marriage garland around his shoulders, her face bright with a joy that filled the hall.

When angry rivals surged forward, Bhima and Arjuna stood firm while Krishna smiled and calmed the kings with his word, recognizing the brothers at last. The Pandavas returned home with Draupadi, their new sister and wife joining them to Drupada's powerful house, and hope warmed the road ahead.

stories.title: Yudhishthira Answers the Yaksha
stories.source: Mahabharata — Vana Parva, Kisari Mohan Ganguli translation
body: In a quiet forest lake, Nakula, Sahadeva, Arjuna, and Bhima one by one ignore a hidden voice guarding the water and fall still upon the ground. When Yudhishthira arrives and hears the warning, he pauses to listen, honoring the unseen presence before he himself drinks.

He answers each question of the yaksha with steady thought on duty, wisdom, and the path of the good, and is offered the chance to bring back a single brother. Yudhishthira chooses Nakula, so that both of his fathers' wives will still have a living son, and the yaksha smiles at his fairness.

The guardian reveals himself as Dharma, Yudhishthira's own divine father, and gently restores all four brothers to life. The Pandavas rise together at the lake's edge, renewed and reunited, and walk on through the forest as a whole family once more.
